concepts.name: Memory Hierarchy and Locality
facts: The memory hierarchy exploits temporal and spatial locality by using fast, small, expensive memory for frequent data and slow, large, cheap memory for less frequent data.

Temporal locality means a piece of data is quickly reused in the future (e.g., loops), while spatial locality means neighbors of the current access tend to be accessed soon (e.g., arrays). High-speed caches capture these localities to address the memory wall, and the hierarchy is useful when a small, active subset of the working set receives most accesses.
For frequent data: use fast but expensive and small memory (e.g., cache).
For not frequent data: use slow but cheap and large memory (e.g., main memory, disk).
Temporal locality: data is quickly reused in the future, e.g., loops.
Spatial locality: neighbors of current access tend to be accessed in the future, e.g., arrays.

Miss penalty = access time + data size / bandwidth.
Example: 1-cycle hit, 10% miss rate, 300-cycle penalty gives AMAT = 1 + 0.1 × 300 = 31 cycles.

concepts.name: SRAM vs. DRAM
facts: SRAM stores bits in stable transistor circuits (6 transistors/bit, low power, used in caches and register files), while DRAM stores bits as charge on tiny capacitors (1 transistor/bit, cheap, needs rewriting and refresh, used in DDR/GDDR/HBM).

SRAM reads precharge bit and bitbar to Vdd, select the row, let the cell pull one line, and use a sense amp to detect the difference; DRAM reads precharge the bit line, share charge between cell and bit line, and sense very small voltage changes (~10–100k electrons), restoring the value on write. DRAM addresses are multiplexed with RAS for the upper half and CAS for the lower half.
SRAM: 6 transistors/bit, expensive, retains bit with low power (423mV for 45nm).
DRAM: 1 transistor/bit, cheap, must be re-written after read and periodically refreshed (each row simultaneously).
DRAM address lines are multiplexed: RAS = upper half, CAS = lower half.
Usage: SRAM in caches and register files; DRAM in DDR/GDDR/HBM.

A rank combines DRAM chips into the channel data width, and multiple ranks share the channel while the controller selects a rank and schedules requests across its banks.
